title: Publish-Subscribe
concept: Publish-subscribe lets a producer announce that something happened without knowing who needs to hear it: every subscriber gets its own copy of each message. A queue hands each message to one consumer; pub-sub hands it to every subscription, and only inside a subscription do consumers share the work. That makes it easy to add readers later, but each subscription now has its own backlog, its own failures and its own idea of order, so the design has to say what a subscriber can count on.

points: Publish-subscribe lets a producer announce that something happened without knowing who needs to hear it: every subscription gets its own copy of each message.
A queue hands each message to one consumer; pub-sub hands it to every subscription, and only inside a subscription do consumers share the work.
Spotify gives each kind of message its own topic and pipeline, so a noisy or blocked kind delays only itself.
Uber's Consumer Proxy gives up order inside a partition so any worker can take any message, which suits work where order does not matter.

figures.label: over 8 million events per second global peak at the end of Q1 2019
over 300 microservices use Kafka for pub-sub message queueing

prerequisiteReasons.message-queues: Publish-subscribe takes from message queues the lease, the acknowledgement and at-least-once delivery, now applied to each subscription separately.

posts.title: Spotify's Event Delivery: Life in the Cloud
posts.ageNote: From November 2019. It is here for a fundamental that has not changed: giving every kind of event its own topic and pipeline so one noisy or blocked kind cannot hold up the rest. The post itself says Spotify was rolling out a next-generation system, and no newer source cited here confirms this setup is still in use, so the figures, the VM counts and the choice of Cloud Pub/Sub may have changed.

digest.problem: Spotify moved its infrastructure to Google Cloud Platform in 2015 and had to redesign Event Delivery, the system that carries every event about users and operations from clients and hundreds of systems to storage for analysis. Royalty payments, company metrics and A/B test results depend on it. The earlier system was built on Kafka; after running the Cloud Pub/Sub version for 2.5 years, the post describes what worked and what did not.
digest.constraints: Some events are business critical, such as the one emitted when a user finishes a track, which is used to pay royalties and to count active users, and they carry external delivery and quality SLAs. Volume ranges from a few hundred events an hour to more than a million a second, and event size from a few bytes to tens of kilobytes. The new system also had to pass strict auditing, and it kept the old producing and consuming interface so both systems could run side by side.

walkthrough.explanation: An Event Service parses each event, recognises its type, rejects malformed or unrecognised events, and publishes the rest to Cloud Pub/Sub.
Every event type gets its own topic, its own ETL process and its own final storage. Types are rated high, medium or low importance, with an SLO for each: a few hours, 24 hours and 72 hours.
Delivered events are written into immutable hourly buckets per type, so a noisy, broken or blocked type delays only itself.
Cloud Pub/Sub is the backbone, with Cloud Storage for data, Compute Engine for the ETL, and Dataproc for deduplication. Close to 15 microservices run on around 2,500 VMs.

Business-critical event types moved first, with both systems running in parallel to compare that all data arrived. Traffic went to the new system at 100% in one day, and the Kafka-based system was shut down in February 2017.
Teams define and emit new event types without involving the delivery team. A central composer creates the topic, subscription, ETL cluster, schema, SLO and monitoring for each one.

tradeoffs.chosen: Managed Cloud Pub/Sub as the backbone, with a separate topic, ETL and storage for each event type, and liveness over lateness.
tradeoffs.rejected: The earlier Kafka-based system, Dataflow for the ETL, and Google's official Java client libraries at the time.
tradeoffs.why: The post says the operational difficulties of the Kafka system taught the team that not all events are equal, so it isolated them as early as possible. Dataflow looked right for the ETL but failed when the proof of concept was productionised, and the official Pub/Sub client libraries were not ready for the team's use and scale, so Spotify wrote its own and used them for more than a year before switching to Google's.

digest.failures: Dataflow did not survive productionising. The first Pub/Sub client libraries failed for Spotify's scale. The default GCE health checker replaced an unhealthy machine with a new one of the same name, which the Puppet certificate authority rejected, so Spotify wrote its own health checker. Autoscaling made fleet-wide deploys take up to three hours, and giving engineers data for free led to waste, which the team now limits with short cost-saving sprints.
digest.takeaways: Give each kind of message its own topic and pipeline, so a noisy or blocked kind delays only itself, and rank the kinds by importance so incidents are handled in order. The post does not discuss delivery guarantees or ordering, so it shows how a pub-sub system is split up and run, not what a subscriber may assume about duplicates or sequence. Plan capacity early: the post saw data grow an order of magnitude faster than service traffic.

posts.title: Enabling Seamless Kafka Async Queuing with Consumer Proxy
posts.ageNote: From August 2021. It is here for a fundamental that has not changed: a log partition limits how many consumers can work in parallel, and per-message work needs something between the log and the workers. No newer Uber source cited here confirms Consumer Proxy is unchanged, so the figures, such as 12 million messages a second and 300 services, may have changed.

digest.problem: Uber runs one of the largest Apache Kafka deployments, and more than 300 microservices use it for pub-sub message queueing between services. After five years of scaling that use from 1 million to 12 million messages a second, the team hit two problems: partitions limited how many consumers could work in parallel, and one slow or unprocessable message blocked every message behind it in the same partition.
digest.constraints: Kafka assumes ordered consumption: a partition is read by one consumer in a group, which processes a message, commits it, and only then takes the next. Most queueing at Uber does not use autocommit, because at-least-once processing is required and a use like billing cannot lose data. Uber has over 1000 microservices in Go, Java, Python and NodeJS, and upgrading client libraries across them usually takes months.

walkthrough.explanation: The post's hypothetical billing example: if each call to a payment provider takes 1 second, a topic needs 1,000 partitions to process 1,000 events a second. A cluster sustains about 200,000 partitions, which would cap it at about 200 such topics, while each partition could carry far more than the 1 message a second it is used for.

walkthrough.step: Put a push proxy between Kafka and services
walkthrough.explanation: Consumer Proxy fetches messages with the Kafka protocol and pushes each one to a consumer service instance over gRPC. The service replies with a status code, and the proxy commits to Kafka when it is safe.

walkthrough.step: Process in parallel inside a partition
walkthrough.explanation: One proxy node reads a partition but fans a batch out to any number of service instances, so the instance count no longer depends on the partition count.

walkthrough.step: Acknowledge one message at a time
walkthrough.explanation: Services acknowledge single messages out of order. The proxy tracks acknowledged offsets and commits to Kafka only when everything before them is acknowledged, so a slow message does not stop later ones from being fetched.

A service can reply with an error code that makes the proxy save the message to a dead letter queue topic, where it counts as negatively acknowledged. Users can later replay it to the service or discard it.
Each service sets a tracker size and a processing timeout, the proxy adjusts its push rate from the status codes, and a circuit breaker stops pushing when a service is fully down.

tradeoffs.chosen: A proxy that pushes messages to services, with out-of-order acknowledgement, a dead letter queue and flow control, built on an internal clustering framework.
tradeoffs.rejected: A client-side library wrapper (tried earlier), Confluent Kafka Rest Proxy, and Kafka Connect.
tradeoffs.why: A library would have to be written and upgraded in four languages across over 1000 services, and a rolling restart could set off group rebalance storms. Kafka Rest Proxy kept one partition per proxy instance and had no single-message acknowledgement or dead letter queue. Kafka Connect was passed over because Uber wanted tighter control of rebalancing for its latency target and bounded consumption to replay from the dead letter queue.

digest.failures: Out-of-order commit alone still has limits: messages can be duplicated after a group rebalance, and a poison pill can never be acknowledged, so it blocks commits behind it, which is what the dead letter queue fixes. Uber accepts the duplicates because consumer services usually deduplicate. The post also says the flow-control settings are hard to tune, and plans adaptive flow control.
digest.takeaways: A queue and a log want different things from consumers: ordered, one-at-a-time reading ties parallelism to partitions, while queue work wants any worker to take any message. A push proxy buys that parallelism by giving up order inside a partition, so use it only where order does not matter. Acknowledge singly, commit only a gapless run, and give poison pills somewhere to go. The 10 second P99 is a target, not a result.

comparison:
Both put a topic between publishers and the systems that read it, and were run at large scale, so both are about what happens on the reading side once the topic exists: backlogs, slow readers and bad messages. Spotify's post is from 2019 and Uber's from 2021, and both may have changed since.

Spotify's readers are ETL jobs that write events to storage, so it solved isolation: one topic, one ETL and one store per event type, with a service level for each importance, so a blocked type delays only itself. Uber's readers are services that call other services for each message, so it solved parallelism: a proxy between Kafka and the services that gives up ordering inside a partition so any instance can take any message.

Spotify's evidence is about volume, with a peak above 8 million events a second and over 500 event types, and its post does not discuss delivery guarantees or ordering. Uber's evidence is about why partitions limit throughput, and the post notes that duplicates are tolerated because consumers deduplicate. Its P99 under 10 seconds is a target, not a measurement.

glossary.definition: A named stream that publishers send messages to, without knowing who reads it.
The part of a system that sends a message to a topic.
One reader's view of a topic, with its own position and backlog. Every subscription gets every message.
A consumer that receives messages through a subscription.
Delivering one published message to every subscription on its topic.
A slice of a topic. Order is usually kept only inside one partition, and a partition is read by one consumer of a group at a time.
Consumers that share one subscription, so each message goes to only one of them.
A consumer's signal that it finished a message. Without one in time, the message is delivered again.
Every message arrives, possibly more than once, so consumers must be safe to run twice.
A place where a message that keeps failing is parked, so it stops blocking the messages behind it.
One slow or unprocessable message holding up every message behind it.

mistakes: Mixing up a subscription and a consumer. Two copies of one service in separate subscriptions each process every message, and two different services sharing one subscription each see only some of them.
Assuming one global order. A topic usually keeps order only inside a partition, so events that must stay in sequence need the same key, and a subscriber that sees them out of order has to cope.

Assuming each message arrives exactly once, and having no plan for a message that always fails. Retries mean duplicates, and one bad message can block everything behind it unless it is parked in a dead letter queue.

why.outcome: After this you can explain why systems publish events to a topic instead of calling each interested system directly.
why.body:
When an order is placed, billing, email, analytics and fraud checks all want to know. If the order service calls each one, it must know them all, a slow one slows the order, and adding another means changing the order service.

Publish-subscribe reverses this. The order service publishes one message to a topic and moves on. Each interested system subscribes and gets its own copy at its own pace. A queue hands each message to one consumer; pub-sub hands it to every subscription. The price is that each subscription now has its own backlog and its own failures, and you have to decide what order and how many deliveries a subscriber can rely on.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture a message fanning out to subscriptions and telling a queue from pub-sub.
mentalModel.body:
Think of a magazine. The publisher prints each issue once and sends it to the topic. Every subscription is a separate subscriber, and each gets its own copy, so the publisher never needs to know who they are or how many there are. Each subscriber also keeps its own bookmark: one can be three issues behind without affecting the others.

A queue is the special case of one subscription that several workers share, so each message goes to just one of them. Pub-sub is many such subscriptions side by side. When a subscriber takes a message it must acknowledge it; if it does not in time, the message comes back, which is at-least-once delivery.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can walk through publishing, fan-out, acknowledgement, ordering and failure handling.

steps.explanation: The publisher sends a message and waits for the topic to confirm it is stored. It does not know who will read it.
The topic gives every subscription its own copy. Each subscription tracks its own position, so readers never wait for each other.
Consumers in one subscription, often called a consumer group, split its messages, so each message goes to one of them. This is the queue behaviour, and it is how you scale a single reader.

A consumer acknowledges when it has finished. With no acknowledgement in time the message is delivered again. That is at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be safe to run twice. At-most-once is the opposite choice: no repeats, but a crash can lose a message. Exactly-once is usually at-least-once with deduplication.

A topic is split into partitions for scale, and order is usually kept only inside one partition. Events that must stay in sequence share a key, so they land in the same partition. Parallel readers across partitions have no shared order.
A message that cannot be processed blocks the messages behind it in its partition. After a few retries it is moved to a dead letter queue so the rest can proceed.

workedExample.outcome: After this you can follow one event through three subscriptions and see where a slow reader, a new reader and a duplicate show up.

steps.explanation: The order service publishes OrderPlaced with the customer's ID as the key, and returns to the customer without waiting for anyone.
Email, billing and analytics each get their own copy. Billing and email each run several workers that share their subscription.
The email provider is slow, so the email subscription's backlog grows. Billing and analytics are unaffected because each has its own position.
An email worker sends a message and crashes before acknowledging. The message is delivered again, so the worker records each order ID it has emailed and skips the second send.
Because the key is the customer ID, one customer's events reach one partition and are read in order. Different customers are read in parallel with no order between them.
A new subscription starts reading the topic. The order service is not changed or redeployed.

lesson.mistakesOutcome: After this you can avoid three mistakes with pub-sub.
lesson.checkOutcome: After this you can tell whether you understood the concept before reading the posts.

quiz.question: An order service must tell billing, email and analytics that an order was placed, and a fourth system will need it next year. Which design avoids changing the order service later?
options: The order service calls each system directly, and a new call is added later for the fourth system
The order service publishes to a topic and each system has its own subscription
All of the systems share one subscription, so any system can read any order message
quiz.why: The publisher only knows the topic, and every subscription receives every message, so a new system just adds a subscription.
wrong: The order service has to know every receiver, so adding a fourth means changing and redeploying it.
Systems sharing one subscription split the messages between them, so each would see only some orders.

quiz.question: Three workers read from the same subscription. One message is published. What happens?
options: All three workers receive a copy
The message is split into three parts
quiz.why: Workers inside one subscription share its messages, so each message goes to one of them. That is the queue behaviour inside pub-sub.
wrong: Copies go to separate subscriptions, not to workers sharing one; three copies would triple the work.
A message is delivered whole; it is never divided between workers.

quiz.question: Two subscriptions read one topic. The email subscription falls far behind. What happens to billing?
options: Billing slows down to match email, because both subscriptions share one position in the topic
Messages are dropped for both, because the topic discards anything a subscription has not read
Billing keeps receiving messages at its own pace while email builds a backlog
quiz.why: Each subscription has its own position and backlog, so a slow reader delays only itself.
wrong: Subscriptions do not wait for each other, so one slow reader cannot set the pace for another.
Messages stay in the topic until each subscription acknowledges them; one reader falling behind does not discard them for the other.

quiz.question: A subscriber crashes after processing a message but before acknowledging it, under at-least-once delivery. What should you expect?
options: The message is delivered again, so processing it twice must be safe
The message is lost, because the crash happened before it was acknowledged
The message is skipped for good, because the work had already been done
quiz.why: With no acknowledgement the system cannot tell the work was done, so it delivers again. The consumer has to be idempotent.
wrong: At-least-once delivery exists to prevent loss, so an unacknowledged message is not dropped.
Nothing marks it finished, so it is not skipped; it comes back.

quiz.question: Events for one customer must be handled in order, while many consumers work in parallel. What do you do?
options: Use one global order across the whole topic
Key events by customer so they land in one partition, and rely on order only inside it
Let consumers process events in whatever order they arrive
quiz.why: Order is kept inside a partition, and a key sends all of a customer's events to the same one, while other customers run in parallel on other partitions.
wrong: A single global order would mean one reader at a time, which removes the parallelism you wanted.
Without a key, a customer's events can spread over partitions and arrive out of sequence.

quiz.question: One message can never be processed, and it blocks the messages behind it. What fixes this?
options: Retry it a limited number of times, then move it to a dead letter queue and carry on
quiz.why: Parking the failing message lets the others proceed, and it can be inspected and replayed later.
wrong: Retrying forever keeps the block in place and still never succeeds.
Deleting the subscription throws away the backlog of good messages as well.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe how two companies organised and read from topics at large scale, and what each post leaves out.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can explain the difference between isolating readers by event type and adding parallelism to a partitioned log.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can apply pub-sub to a slow call, design the topics for a notification system, and plan for ten times the load.

exercises.prompt: A checkout service calls the email, inventory and analytics services in turn. The analytics service is slow, so checkouts time out. What do you change?
exercises.answer: Publish an OrderPlaced event to a topic and return to the customer. Give email, inventory and analytics a subscription each. A slow analytics service now builds its own backlog instead of delaying checkout. Make each consumer safe to run twice, because delivery is at-least-once.
exercises.tradeoffs: Analytics and email now lag behind checkout, and you run a topic and three consumers. Anything checkout must know before it responds, such as stock, still needs a direct call.
wrongAnswers: Raising the timeout on the analytics call.
Putting all three services in one subscription so they share the work.
Assuming each service will see each event exactly once.

exercises.prompt: Design the topics for a notification system with a few high-value events, such as password resets, and many noisy ones, such as page views. How do you stop the noisy ones hurting the important ones?
exercises.answer: Use a separate topic and subscription per event type, or per importance level, with its own consumers and its own backlog alert. A burst of page views then fills only its own backlog. Rank the types so that, in an incident, the critical ones are drained first, and key events that need order, such as one user's password resets, by user ID.
exercises.tradeoffs: More topics to name, monitor and clean up. Spotify automated this with a service that creates the topic, subscription, schema and monitoring for each new event type.
wrongAnswers: One topic for everything with a type field, read by one shared group.
Dropping page views when load rises, without telling their owners.
Using one partition to keep a global order.

exercises.prompt: Traffic grows ten times. Each message needs a call to another service that takes 100 ms, and the topic has a fixed number of partitions, so adding consumers does not help. What do you do?
exercises.answer: With one message at a time per partition, throughput is bounded by partitions divided by call time. Options: add partitions, which costs a rebalance and changes keys' placement; or put a dispatcher between the topic and the workers that fans messages out to many instances, as Uber's Consumer Proxy does. That needs single-message acknowledgement, a dead letter queue and flow control, and it gives up order inside a partition.
exercises.tradeoffs: More partitions keep order but have limits. A dispatcher scales workers independently but loses order and adds a component to run, and duplicates can appear after a rebalance.
wrongAnswers: Adding consumers beyond the number of partitions and expecting them all to get work.
Turning on autocommit to go faster, which loses messages on a restart.
Processing messages out of order for events that must stay in sequence.

next.outcome: After this you can pick the next topic that builds on this one.
next.body: Event-driven architecture builds on pub-sub, and it is the next topic on the map. When a subscriber is overwhelmed, Rate Limiting and Circuit Breakers cover how to protect it; Uber's proxy used a circuit breaker for exactly that.
